results.title: USMCA's Core Dimensions and Georgia's Automotive Industry
results.content: June 7, 2026 - USMCA rules on Regional Value Content have driven Georgia's shift toward EV production, creating a tension between maintaining investment stability and pursuing flexible reforms. Regional Value Content (RVC): The USMCA mandates that a higher percentage of a vehicle's components must be produced in North America to qualify for zero tariffs. This has incentivized manufacturers to move supply chains away from overseas markets and into the North American corridor.

results.content: Georgia’s success in attracting EV companies to build large scale final assembly plants is creating opportunity for other states in the region to benefit from the development of an end-to-end battery supply chain. States across the region are leaning into their individual strengths to take advantage of new opportunities afforded from different parts of the value chain, including mineral sourcing, mid-stream manufacturing, and battery recycling. This growth across Georgia and the broader [...] manufacturing investment, the state is a key market for batteries produced locally. Since 2018, Georgia has announced over $27.3 billion in investments to manufacture electric mobility products, including Kia’s West Point manufacturing facility, Hyundai’s Bryan County Metaplant, and Rivian’s upcoming Atlanta East Coast headquarters and Social Circle, GA manufacturing facility. This rapid growth in manufacturing has attracted suppliers to the state and sent a clear demand signal for the region [...] and the broader region’s economy is fundamental to supporting the long-term success of the robust EV ecosystem in the state. Each state in the region has a role to play in establishing a cluster of new technology development and industry growth and stands to gain significant job creation and economic benefits.

EV sales will dip — Higher prices = fewer buyers. Expect 10-20% sales decline in July-December 2026

Starting in June 2026, a 25% tariff on imported vehicles and auto parts will fundamentally change EV pricing in America. This isn’t theoretical — it’s happening NOW, and it will cost EV buyers thousands of dollars more. [...] 25% tariff on imported vehicles — Effective June 3, 2026. Applies to cars assembled outside the US, including imported Tesla vehicles, BMWs, Audis, and most EVs.
 25% tariff on auto parts — Effective May 2026 (phased). Applies to batteries, semiconductors, motors, and components imported from outside North America.
 Who gets hit: Tesla (imports from China & Mexico), BMW, Audi, Mercedes, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Kia, and any EV with imported components.

results.title: Battery Pack Tariffs: What OEMs Need to Know in 2026
results.content:
### Mid-2025: The Policy Accelerates

Section 232 investigations into battery-related imports were announced, signaling additional potential tariff actions beyond existing measures. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated federal EV purchase incentives – the $7,500 new EV tax credit, the $4,000 used EV credit, and the commercial fleet EV credit – reducing downstream demand pressure but doing nothing to reduce upstream input costs for battery manufacturers.

### 2026: FEOC Compliance Kicks In [...] Key Context: The Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) in February 2026, but the administration continued pursuing battery-related trade barriers through other legal authorities including Section 232 investigations, while maintaining existing measures including a 10 percent import surcharge under Section 122. The regulatory environment remains fluid.

## 2. The Real Cost of Battery Pack Tariffs on OEM Sourcing [...] Battery pack tariffs changed the rules overnight. Tariffs that OEM engineers and procurement managers once treated as background noise have become the single most disruptive force in US battery pack sourcing. Since January 2025, the cost of importing battery components from China has risen by as much as 69 percent. For manufacturers who built their supply chains around offshore pricing, the math no longer works.

results.title: What The Car Tariffs Mean for EVs
results.content:
25% tariffs will be applied to imports of automobiles and automobile parts
 These tariffs will be applied to all imported passenger vehicles, light trucks, and key automobile parts (engines, transmissions, powertrain parts, and electrical components), with processes to expand if deemed necessary
 Imports under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement can certify their US content; the tariffs will only apply to the value of the non-US content [...] For example, the Ford Mustang Mach-E sources 18% of its parts from Mexico and 51% from China, with only 26% coming from the US or Canada, not to mention having a final assembly in Mexico. The Chevy Blazer EV and Equinox EV share a similar story, with 18% of their parts coming from China and a final assembly in Mexico. If you are interested in how the tariffs may affect a specific vehicle, a full list of part sourcing and manufacturing locations can be found here. [...] ### Implications for the Future of the American Auto Industry

Manufacturing Supply Chains

President Trump has stated that part of his motive behind the tariffs is to encourage the American automotive industry to source and build in America. As White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt put it, “He told them they should get on it, start investing, start moving, shift production here to the United States of America, where they will pay no tariff. That is the ultimate goal.”
